<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Kilometer-scale convection shapes precipitation extremes, tropical
organization, and cloud feedbacks, but most global atmospheric models
approximate these processes at 25–100 km resolution.
Global storm-resolving physics models resolve convective systems explicitly, but at a cost—roughly one MWh per simulated day on exascale supercomputers—that limits long-duration simulation.
We introduce STRATA (Storm-resolving Tile-based autoRegressive Atmosphere Transformer Architecture), the first autoregressive AI emulator for global storm-resolving atmospheric dynamics.
STRATA is trained on the highest-resolution atmospheric dataset yet used for global AI emulation:
17 days of SCREAM physics-model output at 4.9-km resolution (<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}25</annotation></semantics></math> million grid cells) sampled every 10 minutes.
Our central premise is that on 10-minute timescales atmospheric dynamics are predominantly local, so training on small spatial tiles trades scarce global temporal samples for abundant local spatial samples and enables global rollout via overlapping-tile blending.
STRATA combines 3D patch embedding and local 3D neighborhood attention, a novel Stereographic Rotary Position Embedding
(StereoRoPE) for grid-invariant encoding, and a pixel-space
de-aliasing decoder that suppresses patch-scale rollout artifacts.
An iso-FLOP scaling study reveals that km-scale emulation requires <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\sim}10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}10\times</annotation></semantics></math> more FLOPs per grid point than coarse-resolution AI weather models, consistent with the higher information density of convective-scale dynamics.
Trained on only 17 days of data, STRATA produces stable 24-hour global rollouts with realistic km-scale dynamics across diverse regimes, though large-scale biases develop with lead time.
It achieves 48 simulation days per megawatt-hour—about 50 times better energy efficiency than the SCREAM physics model—and 741 simulated days per wall-clock day at 512 H100 GPUs.
Code and dataset are publicly available (Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Data and Code Availability ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
  
</div><span id="footnotex2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Corresponding author(s): <span id="footnotex2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">zeyuanh@nvidia.com</span>, <span id="footnotex2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">nbrenowitz@nvidia.com</span>.</span></span></span>
<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/overview_paper6_gt_vs_forecast_step071.png" id="S0.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/238;" width="471" height="238" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S0.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Twelve-hour STRATA rollout compared with SCREAM.</span>
Top: near-surface specific humidity and rain intensity at +12 h from STRATA (left) and the
corresponding SCREAM reference simulation (right) on the native 4.9-km output
grid (<math id="S0.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6\times 2048^{2}\approx 25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>2048</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6\times 2048^{2}\approx 25</annotation></semantics></math> M horizontal cells). The colored
boxes in the global SCREAM panel mark the zoom locations.
Bottom: zoomed comparisons across six representative regimes. Row 1: STRATA forecast. Row 2: SCREAM ground truth at native 4.9-km
resolution. Humidity colors in the zoom panels are independently
rescaled for each location to emphasize local structure. Scale bars are
100 km.
Supplementary videos of the full 24-hour rollout are available at
<a href="https://zydlszh.github.io/strata-supp/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://zydlszh.github.io/strata-supp/</a>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Long-range atmospheric simulation is
among the most challenging computational workflows in science.
Weather and climate depend on processes spanning more than ten orders of magnitude in space, from microphysics interactions between cloud droplets and raindrops to planetary-scale circulation, and physical fidelity requires accurately representing all of them.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, the finest scales are typically approximated by closed-form parameterizations rather than simulated explicitly, introducing substantial uncertainty in long-range projections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. To reduce this uncertainty, state-of-the-art physics models push to ever-finer grids that explicitly resolve convective storms rather than approximating them—currently reaching <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}1</annotation></semantics></math> km globally. These models, known as global storm-resolving models (GSRMs; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a></cite>; Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Background: Global Storm-Resolving Models ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>) offer unprecedented realism, but remain staggeringly expensive: the leading GSRMs achieve a throughput of roughly 1 simulated day (SD) per MWh on exascale supercomputers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, roughly 2.5 SD per ton of CO<sub id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub">2</sub> emitted or 1.3 SD per passenger for a one-way coach flight from Seattle to New York.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">AI emulators promise the same fidelity at lower cost because their core computations are more arithmetically-intense and suited to modern hardware accelerators. While traditional atmospheric solvers are memory-bandwidth bound—spending most of their time moving data rather than computing—transformer-based architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> operate on dense, low-precision matrix multiplications that saturate GPU compute units. Coarse-resolution global atmospheric emulators and limited-domain km-scale emulators have realized this efficiency gain in their respective regimes (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Related Work ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) but achieving autoregressive rollout at both <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">global and km-scale</span>, the only regime that can replace a full-resolution GSRM, remains an unsolved challenge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Reaching this milestone is hindered by several challenges that do not arise when using AI to simulate weather at coarse resolution. Convective dynamics are 3D, have elevated information density, and require 10-min (36<math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> more) sampling in time and 4.9 km (25<math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> more) sampling in space to constrain.
This raises acute computational challenges.
A given day of GSRM data occupies thousands of times more memory than a day of the ERA5 dataset. Such high resolution data is difficult to store on disk and activation memory-use during training becomes prohibitive.
The upshot is a problem that demands especially scalable training strategies working backwards from an ambitious global inference goal—rapidly evolving 25M atmospheric horizontal grid cells globally.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce STRATA (Storm-resolving Tile-based autoRegressive Atmosphere Transformer Architecture), to our knowledge the first AI emulator to demonstrate successful autoregressive rollout at global km-scale. Its central premise is that atmospheric phenomena on 10-minute timescales are predominantly local, so a tile-based training strategy can convert temporally scarce global simulations into spatially abundant samples, with overlapping tile blending reassembling a coherent global state at inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Our key technical solutions to the challenges of training a high-throughput global high resolution model include:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tile-based training of global auto-regressive models.</span> The activation memory bottleneck is overcome by training on crops. Only inference is global.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3D local-attention backbone.</span> 3D patch tokenization and neighborhood attention further exploit atmospheric locality for efficient roll-out.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stereographic Rotary Position Embedding (StereoRoPE).</span> Grid-invariant position encoding via stereographic projection, enabling consistent spatial representation across tile locations and arbitrary grid topologies.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patch de-aliasing.</span> A spectral stability analysis of patch-embedded architectures and a pixel-space dealiasing decoder that greatly reduces the resulting checkerboard artifacts.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Additional accomplishments are as follows. STRATA produces stable 24-hour rollouts reproducing realistic km-scale dynamics across diverse weather regimes. Scaling analysis reveals <math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\sim}10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}10\times</annotation></semantics></math> more FLOPs are needed per grid point than coarse-resolution forecasting, with an information-theoretic explanation based on the higher entropy of convective-scale data. Most importantly, inference runs at a throughput of 48 simulated days per MWh—about 50 times better energy efficiency than SCREAM—and scales to 741 simulated days per wall-clock day at 512 H100 GPUs (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Scaling transformers for high-entropy data ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>a).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Coarse-resolution emulators</span>
Global AI weather models now rival operational forecasts at <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}0.25^{\circ}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><msup><mn>0.25</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}0.25^{\circ}</annotation></semantics></math> resolution and 6-hour timesteps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, and several coarse-resolution atmosphere emulators have produced stable multi-decadal to century-long rollouts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>. However, these systems operate at resolutions at least an order of magnitude coarser than kilometer scale and therefore cannot simulate explicit convective-scale phenomena.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Regional km-scale emulators.</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Flora and Potvin [24]</a></cite> show that realistic convection can be generated with a deterministic model when the resolution is fine enough in space (3-km) and time (10-minute). However, their simulations are limited to spatial extents of <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="($1000\text{\,}\mathrm{km}$)^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1000</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi class="ltx_unit">km</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">($1000\text{\,}\mathrm{km}$)^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and are only rolled out to two hours. Other regional emulators have been trained on 1-hour time resolution data, but either become blurry <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> or require expensive diffusion sampling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Super-resolution.</span>
Generative diffusion models offer a complementary path to km-scale output by conditioning on coarse atmospheric states rather than rolling out autoregressively—producing km-scale details diagnostically as a function of the coarse input <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. Inspiring our approach, global coverage is made tractable via patch-based training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. While practical for inpainting realistic details when trained on undersampled datasets, diffusion-based generation is purely downscale, so cannot model the two-way feedback between fine and large scales that we are after.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spherical architectures.</span>
Faithfully representing data on the sphere is a core challenge for global atmospheric emulators, motivating a range of geometry-aware
architectures mostly targeting resolutions of <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\geq}0.25^{\circ}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><msup><mn>0.25</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\geq}0.25^{\circ}</annotation></semantics></math>; scaling to km-scale grids remains an open problem. For example, Spherical Fourier Neural Operators <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite> replace standard FFTs with spherical harmonic transforms for globally equivariant weather modeling <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}0.25^{\circ}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><msup><mn>0.25</mn><mo>∘</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}0.25^{\circ}</annotation></semantics></math>, but by using global basis functions they preclude our memory-saving local training strategy.
Alternately, MeshGraphNet-based architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> avoid polar geometric distortions and can be run globally or locally, but suffer from low throughput because they are based on sparse message passing operations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Proposed Method</h2>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/method-overview-schematic.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/322;" width="471" height="322" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">STRATA method overview.</span>
<span id="S3.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a,b)</span> STRATA learns 10-minute updates from local SCREAM tiles and
applies the same model globally using overlapping tiles that are blended into a
continuous rollout; Duo-grid halo padding supplies geometrically consistent
context near cubed-sphere face boundaries.
<span id="S3.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span> The tile update model combines 3D patch embedding, local attention
mechanisms, and a pixel-space de-aliasing decoder adapted from PixelDiT.
<span id="S3.F2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(d,e)</span> Stereographic Rotary Position Embedding (StereoRoPE) projects
each tile to a local stereographic frame and rotates vector inputs into the
same tile-centered frame, providing grid-invariant position information for
the transformer.


</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Tile-based training and inference</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train on independent <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128\times 128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>128</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128\times 128</annotation></semantics></math> tiles (<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}576" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>576</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}576</annotation></semantics></math> km across)—sufficient to capture all physically relevant signals in a
10-minute step, since even acoustic waves propagate only <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}200</annotation></semantics></math> km per step—using the many spatial tiles in each
global snapshot as training samples to trade scarce temporal coverage for abundant spatial samples (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>a).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At inference, STRATA is applied globally by decomposing each cubed-sphere face into overlapping tiles, processing them independently, and blending the overlap regions into a continuous global state (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>b). For tiles near cube-face boundaries, accurately predicting state changes requires atmospheric context from the adjacent face. These cross-face neighbors cannot be used directly, however, because the cubed-sphere grid orientation changes discontinuously at face boundaries, and at corners where three faces meet, naive padding is geometrically ill-defined. Duo-Grid halo padding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> addresses this by extending each face’s equiangular grid past its boundary and interpolating neighboring-face values onto this extended grid (yellow shading in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>b), giving boundary tiles a locally coherent neighborhood that the model processes identically to interior tiles. This tile-based inference protocol also enables scalability to a multi-GPU distributed environment, yielding strong scaling efficiency of up to 98.4% from 8 to 512 GPUs and a throughput of 741 simulated days per wall-clock day at 512 GPUs. More inference details are in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Inference ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Architecture</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Km-scale atmospheric dynamics have two properties that shape the
architecture: they are intrinsically 3D and predominantly local on
10-minute timescales.
STRATA addresses these with three components
(Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>c): a 3D patch embedding layer, a
local-attention DiT transformer backbone, and a pixel-space de-aliasing
decoder.
Full architecture specifications are provided in
Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transformer backbone.</span>
The STRATA backbone follows the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> architecture (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>, Figure <a href="#A2.F1" title="Figure S1 ‣ B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a>a), adapted for deterministic atmospheric emulation rather than diffusion sampling. All input fields are concatenated and treated as a single volumetric tensor spanning the horizontal tile and all vertical levels. At a 10-minute timestep, atmospheric interactions are largely local, so we use 3D Neighborhood Attention (NATTEN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>), with stereographic rotary position embeddings (see §<a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Grid-Invariant Position Encoding via Stereographic Projection ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>) inside local <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y,\mathrm{lev})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>lev</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y,\mathrm{lev})</annotation></semantics></math> windows. With a horizontal patch embedding size of 4 and a NATTEN kernel size of 9, each attention window covers <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="36\times 36" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>36</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>36</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">36\times 36</annotation></semantics></math> horizontal native grid cells (<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\approx}160\times 160" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>160</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>160</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\approx}160\times 160</annotation></semantics></math> km). We alternate these blocks with column-wise attention along the vertical dimension to capture processes that are computed column-by-column in SCREAM with no horizontal coupling, such as vertical radiation transfer and cloud microphysics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3D Patch-embedding and computational efficiency.</span>
Like the original DiT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, STRATA uses patch embedding to tokenize the input, grouping <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{h}\times p_{h}\times p_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>v</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{h}\times p_{h}\times p_{v}</annotation></semantics></math> 3D grid cells into a single token before the transformer sees them. Unlike coarse-resolution atmospheric transformers, we treat the vertical dimension as a spatial axis (<math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{v}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{v}=1</annotation></semantics></math>) rather than a channel dimension (<math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{v}=\text{\# of levels})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext># of levels</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{v}=\text{\# of levels})</annotation></semantics></math>. This decision is motivated on both physical and computational grounds—it allows modeling the 3D dynamics of atmospheric convection at the token level and acts as an independent lever for scaling computational complexity, and therefore accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The computational complexity of our architecture, measured in terms of FLOPs, is approximated by <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2NP" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2NP</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of parameters and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> the number of patches <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\propto(p_{v}p_{h}^{2})^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>p</mi><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\propto(p_{v}p_{h}^{2})^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>. The number of parameters <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\propto d^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\propto d^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> is the embedding dimension of the network. From this we see that reducing the vertical patch size to <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{v}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{v}=1</annotation></semantics></math> while holding the embedding dimension fixed increases <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> and the computational complexity of the model overall.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Even for a fixed FLOP budget (<math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\propto N^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∝</mo><msup><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\propto N^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math>) the patch size is an important lever. Reducing <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> improves model FLOP utilization (MFU)—by reducing the size of the activations which scales as <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(Nd)=O(N\sqrt{P})=O(\sqrt{N})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>P</mi></msqrt></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msqrt><mi>N</mi></msqrt><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(Nd)=O(N\sqrt{P})=O(\sqrt{N})</annotation></semantics></math> and in so doing increasing the overall arithmetic intensity of the architecture.
Another benefit of larger patches is that they expand the effective window size of the neighborhood attention at no extra cost, which improves the accuracy. Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Architecture ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>b shows that for constant FLOPs the loss decreases with patch size.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patch instability and pixel-space de-aliasing decoder.</span>
Patch tokenization introduces checkerboard artifacts in rollouts
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>,
most visibly in smooth fields like near-surface temperature.
We argue this is caused by a spectral bias of the patched architecture upon
initialization: the block-diagonal structure of the linearized update operator
gives <math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>, causing patch-scale eigenvectors to dominate the rollout.
A formal stability analysis is provided in
Appendix <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Patch Instability Analysis ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a>.
We mitigate this with a lightweight decoder of PixelDiT pixel
blocks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>; within each block, we replace
the original linear-projection upsampling with bilinear upsampling followed by
depthwise convolutional refinement to enforce continuity across patch boundaries
(Figure <a href="#A2.F1" title="Figure S1 ‣ B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a>b,c).
Figure <a href="#A2.F2" title="Figure S2 ‣ B.3 Patch De-aliasing ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Patch De-aliasing ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>
shows this substantially reduces patch-scale artifacts in 12-hour rollouts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.31248v1/paper_throughput_and_testloss.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/182;" width="429" height="182"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Patch-size and model-size scaling.</span>
<span id="S3.F3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> inference latency vs. FLOPs per forward pass (estimated as
<math id="S3.F3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2NP" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>N</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2NP</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.F3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the token sequence
length and <math id="S3.F3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> the number of parameters) for DiT-S/M/L models with horizontal patch sizes <math id="S3.F3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ps\in\{1,2,4\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ps\in\{1,2,4\}</annotation></semantics></math>;
at equal FLOPs, <math id="S3.F3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ps=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ps=4</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.F3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S3.F3.m15" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than <math id="S3.F3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ps=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ps=1</annotation></semantics></math>.
<span id="S3.F3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> test loss vs. training FLOPs for the same sweep.
Patch size 1 is worse than patch sizes 2 and 4 at equal FLOPs; smaller
models are more compute-efficient at low budgets, while larger models reach
lower loss with sufficient training.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Grid-Invariant Position Encoding via Stereographic Projection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our architecture requires locally rectangular grids for efficiency, but tile-based training requires the same local physical patterns to be represented consistently across the sphere.
Standard embedding strategies for vision transformers, such as axial Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, will fail at this since the same 2D index offset will have a different physical orientation and length depending on the location.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We address this with Stereographic RoPE (StereoRoPE; Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). This approach decouples the coordinate used for RoPE from the discretization of the input data, allowing us to choose the most convenient option for each.
For each tile, we project grid points to a local stereographic tangent plane centered on the tile (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>d) and use the resulting coordinates as RoPE inputs. Because these coordinates approximate physical displacement rather than grid indices, attention patterns can transfer across tile locations and grid topologies. For a tile centered at <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\phi_{0},\lambda_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\phi_{0},\lambda_{0})</annotation></semantics></math>, each token at <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\phi,\lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\phi,\lambda)</annotation></semantics></math> is mapped to tile-centered stereographic coordinates:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\cos c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\cos c</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sin\phi_{0}\sin\phi+\cos\phi_{0}\cos\phi\cos(\lambda-\lambda_{0}),\quad k=\frac{2}{1+\cos c}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sin\phi_{0}\sin\phi+\cos\phi_{0}\cos\phi\cos(\lambda-\lambda_{0}),\quad k=\frac{2}{1+\cos c},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{k}{\ell_{\mathrm{scale}}}\cos\phi\sin(\lambda-\lambda_{0}),\quad y=\frac{k}{\ell_{\mathrm{scale}}}\bigl(\cos\phi_{0}\sin\phi-\sin\phi_{0}\cos\phi\cos(\lambda-\lambda_{0})\bigr)," display="inline" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mi>k</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>scale</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{k}{\ell_{\mathrm{scale}}}\cos\phi\sin(\lambda-\lambda_{0}),\quad y=\frac{k}{\ell_{\mathrm{scale}}}\bigl(\cos\phi_{0}\sin\phi-\sin\phi_{0}\cos\phi\cos(\lambda-\lambda_{0})\bigr),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> is the angular separation from the tile center, <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math> are local East–North coordinates in the tile-centered tangent frame, and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\mathrm{scale}}=\sqrt{4\pi/N_{\mathrm{total}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>scale</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>total</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\mathrm{scale}}=\sqrt{4\pi/N_{\mathrm{total}}}</annotation></semantics></math> normalizes coordinates across resolutions.
These coordinates replace row/column indices as inputs to axial 2D RoPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>. The stereographic projection is chosen because it is conformal, which preserves local angles and facilitates learning vector operators such as advection <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla{q}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> is the velocity and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> a tracer quantity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Because the local East–North frame rotates across the sphere (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>e), raw wind components <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(U,V)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(U,V)</annotation></semantics></math> encode the same physical wind differently at different tile positions—a frame inconsistency that would corrupt the grid-invariant encoding of StereoRoPE. We resolve this by projecting all wind vectors into the single East–North frame defined at the tile center.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Concretely, we form the 3D vector <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}=U\hat{e}+V\hat{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>U</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>e</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}=U\hat{e}+V\hat{n}</annotation></semantics></math> using the per-point unit vectors <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\hat{e},\hat{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>e</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\hat{e},\hat{n})</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\phi,\lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\phi,\lambda)</annotation></semantics></math>, then project onto the tile-center tangent plane spanned by <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\hat{e}_{0},\hat{n}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>e</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\hat{e}_{0},\hat{n}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math>—removing any radial leakage introduced by the change of frame—to obtain tile-center components:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{\perp}=\mathbf{v}-(\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{r}_{0})\hat{r}_{0},\qquad U_{\mathrm{loc}}=\mathbf{v}_{\perp}\cdot\hat{e}_{0},\qquad V_{\mathrm{loc}}=\mathbf{v}_{\perp}\cdot\hat{n}_{0}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>𝐯</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>loc</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>e</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>loc</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>⟂</mo></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>n</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{\perp}=\mathbf{v}-(\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{r}_{0})\hat{r}_{0},\qquad U_{\mathrm{loc}}=\mathbf{v}_{\perp}\cdot\hat{e}_{0},\qquad V_{\mathrm{loc}}=\mathbf{v}_{\perp}\cdot\hat{n}_{0},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{r}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{r}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is the radial unit vector at the tile center.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In early experiments on HEALPix grids <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> (later replaced by the cubed-sphere),
standard RoPE defined on the local grid led to discontinuous wind fields across the boundaries of polar faces, where the local grid changes orientation by 90<sup id="S3.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_sup">∘</sup>.
We further validate grid invariance empirically in
Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Grid invariance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>, demonstrating stable zero-shot rollouts
on unseen grids.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Training Objective and Multi-Step Fine-Tuning</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">STRATA is first trained for one-step prediction with a channel-normalized Smoothed <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> loss (Huber loss with <math id="S3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta=1</annotation></semantics></math>). One-step training minimizes single-step prediction error but allows artifacts to accumulate over autoregressive steps. We therefore fine-tune the model autoregressively for up to four steps, computing the loss on the final prediction. This multi-step fine-tuning substantially suppresses rollout instabilities and is key to stable 24-hour rollouts. Optimization details are in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Training details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate STRATA along two axes: an isoFLOP scaling study to
characterize the compute–accuracy tradeoff at km-scale (§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Scaling transformers for high-entropy data ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>),
and a 24-hour autoregressive rollout to assess emulation fidelity
(§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>).
For the rollout, we adopt metrics appropriate for a chaotic dynamical system:
individual convective cells lose pointwise predictability within a few hours
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>, so structural and statistical
fidelity—precipitation organization, error growth rate, and distributions—
are the meaningful tests, not pointwise agreement.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Dataset</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">STRATA emulates native SCREAM physics-grid output without regridding. While the effective dynamics grid spacing of SCREAM is 3.3 km, its physics output data are saved every 10 minutes on a 4.9-km cubed-sphere grid (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6\times 2048^{2}\approx 25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>6</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>2048</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6\times 2048^{2}\approx 25</annotation></semantics></math> million horizontal grid points) and subsampled from 128 raw SCREAM levels to 24 tropospheric vertical levels (surface to <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}100</annotation></semantics></math> hPa; Figure <a href="#A3.F3" title="Figure S3 ‣ C.1 STRATA Vertical Grid ‣ Appendix C Dataset details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S3</span></a>). We collect 30 days from three non-contiguous SCREAM simulations spanning diverse seasons (October, August, and January) and train on 17 days; rollout evaluation uses 6 held-out initializations at 12-hourly intervals from 2020-10-11 to 2020-10-14 (see Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Training Data ‣ Appendix C Dataset details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>). The model predicts the 10-minute evolution of 3D potential temperature, zonal and meridional wind, vertical velocity, geopotential height, and specific humidity fields, along with near-surface temperature; it also predicts diagnostic surface pressure and precipitation. Forcing inputs include solar zenith angle, surface geopotential, topography, latitude, and land fraction. A complete list of variable information is given in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Input and Output Variables ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Scaling transformers for high-entropy data</h3>
