<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">DiT-S</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">10 min</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1.2</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.6.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1062</span></span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">DiT-M</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">10 min</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4.9</span></span>
<span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.9.1.2.7.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4335</span></span></span>
</span>
</span></p>
<p id="S4.T1.9.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.T1.9.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">TFLOPs/step is per global step for coarse models but per tile for
DiT-S/M; PFLOPs/SD normalizes to a full simulated day globally.</span></p>
</div></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key design question for any emulator is how many FLOPs to allocate per forward pass: more FLOPs increase inference cost, but too few yield poor prediction quality. To understand this effect, we sweep over three iso-FLOP model tiers (DiT-S/M/L) and three horizontal patch sizes (1, 2, 4); see Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Patch-Size and Model-Size Sweep ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a> and Table <a href="#A2.T2" title="Table S2 ‣ B.2 Patch-Size and Model-Size Sweep ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a> for configurations. Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Architecture ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>b shows that the loss decreases predictably with model FLOPs, with smaller models more compute-efficient at low training budgets and larger models reaching lower loss given sufficient training compute—consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al. [37]</a></cite>. Within each tier, the larger patch sized models are more computationally efficient (Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Architecture ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>a). Models with a horizontal patch size <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{h}=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{h}=4</annotation></semantics></math> run <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5</annotation></semantics></math>–<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.9\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{h}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{h}=1</annotation></semantics></math> models at equal FLOPs, with greater gains at smaller FLOP budgets.
Reasonable 24-hour rollout stability begins to emerge at and above the DiT-M tier
(<math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}5</annotation></semantics></math> TFLOP), though biases remain present even at this scale;
models below this threshold exhibit more visible large-scale artifacts
(Figure <a href="#A11.F17" title="Figure S17 ‣ K.4 Model capacity and rollout stability ‣ Appendix K Additional sensitivity test ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S17</span></a>,
Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Further rollout diagnostics ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Consistent with a fundamental increase in underlying entropy, the computational scale required to succeed at simulating realistic convective-scale systems is 10<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> higher than naive extrapolations from established large-scale autoregressive AI weather models would predict based on spatial and temporal resolution differences alone (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Scaling transformers for high-entropy data ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>b). We postulate this increased computational load is required since storm-resolving data (in space and time) has higher information content due to the 3D nature of atmospheric convection. By contrast, the large-scale atmosphere behaves like a two-dimensional fluid, due to the strong impact of the Earth’s rotation at those scales and the large aspect ratio.
A statistical analysis of the compressibility and covariance structure of the km-scale data supports this hypothesis (cf. Appendix <a href="#A10" title="Appendix J Information Entropy: Details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">J</span></a>) and shows that the differential entropy (<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-E_{X}[\log(p(X))]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-E_{X}[\log(p(X))]</annotation></semantics></math>) of 10-minute SCREAM increments (-0.5 bits/dim) is higher than 6-hour 0.25<sup id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sup">∘</sup> ERA5 increments (-6.5 bits/dim). This is a very large difference considering that the maximum entropy distribution with unit variance is the Gaussian (2 bits/dim).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Visualizations of the rollout quality provide a useful qualitative test, if done long after initial condition km-scale memory has vanished. Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that STRATA’s self-generated dynamics resemble the ground truth across multiple phenomena – tropical cyclone,
shallow clouds, midlatitude cold front, Intertropical Convergence Zone,
diurnal island convection, and orographic precipitation. Global videos provide a holistic view (<a href="https://zydlszh.github.io/strata-supp/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://zydlszh.github.io/strata-supp/</a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Quantitative error growth rates affirm good performance for the km-scale. The rainfall fractions skill score <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> (FSS; Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Rollout Metrics ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>) exceeds a persistence baseline (Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>b) indicating nontrivial maintenance of initialized organized rainfall structure. Meanwhile, tropical weather systems traverse the equatorial Indian and West Pacific at the correct speeds (phase tilt of rain streaks in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>a).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Limitations are also apparent in simulating the largest scale circulations. On time scales of 12-24 hours, where macroscale forecast errors dominate, total error growth is too fast (Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>c,d; slope of blue and blue-dashed) relative to expectations of an RMSE doubling-per-day (grey, yellow).
For context, ACE2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, a
coarse-resolution AI atmosphere emulator trained on six decades of global
reanalysis specifically to capture large-scale dynamics, shows
substantially slower error growth; it is not surprising that STRATA,
trained on only 17 days of global km-scale data, does not match ACE2 at synoptic
scales.
Global mean rainfall is biased low by as much as 20% (Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>a); see Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Inference ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> (Figure <a href="#A6.F6" title="Figure S6 ‣ F.2 Spectral filter to control large-scale vertical velocity ‣ Appendix F Inference ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S6</span></a>) for details of vertical velocity filters that ameliorated this. The precipitation amount distribution
(Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>b) broadly matches SCREAM though the
moderate-to-intense rain rates contribute slightly less than in SCREAM,
consistent with the dry bias. Suppressed 12-h spectral power concentrated in the 100-2,000 km length scale regime again implicates imperfect synoptics (Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Physical Realism, Predictability and Statistical Fidelity ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>c). Whether this reflects insufficient training data or a fundamental limitation of the tile-based approach, coupling STRATA with a coarse-resolution global
model is a natural next step.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/paper_hovmoller_fss_rmse_lr_minmax.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/184;" width="476" height="184" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S4.F4.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Predictability diagnostics for 24-hour rollout.</span>
<span id="S4.F4.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> Tropical precipitation over the Indo-Pacific, averaged over
5<sup id="S4.F4.11" class="ltx_sup">∘</sup>S–5<sup id="S4.F4.12" class="ltx_sup">∘</sup>N, shows coherent eastward and westward propagation of
large-scale precipitation structures during STRATA free rollout.
<span id="S4.F4.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> Fractions Skill Score measures neighborhood-scale precipitation
agreement with SCREAM; persistence is shown as an initial-condition memory
reference rather than a competitive baseline.
<span id="S4.F4.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c,d)</span> Root-mean-square error for 850-hPa temperature and 850-hPa
zonal wind on the native 4.9-km grid and after coarsening to
the 1<sup id="S4.F4.15" class="ltx_sup">∘</sup> ACE2 grid. ACE2 is included as a coarse-resolution AI emulator baseline. Lines show the mean over 6 initialization times; shading shows the min–max range across ensemble members.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.31248v1/paper_precip_3panel_step071_w3_n144_s6_inits3_paper6_inits3.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/136;" width="381" height="136"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S4.F5.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Precipitation statistics during rollout.</span>
Solid lines show the mean over three rollouts initialized on different
dates at the same time of day; shading shows the min–max range.
<span id="S4.F5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> Global-mean precipitation over 24-hour rollouts.
<span id="S4.F5.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> Precipitation amount distribution at 12-hour lead time,
showing each rain-rate bin’s contribution to the global mean.
<span id="S4.F5.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span> Spherical-harmonic power spectrum of precipitation at
12-hour lead time.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Grid invariance</h3>

<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/grid_invariance_overlay.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/126;" width="405" height="126" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="S4.F6.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Grid invariance test</span>: near-surface humidity and rain
rate from a 3-hour zero-shot rollout over Indonesia on three grids
of similar nominal resolution—regular latitude–longitude (left),
oblique stereographic rotated 45<sup id="S4.F6.5" class="ltx_sup">∘</sup> (middle), and the native SCREAM
cubed-sphere (right, training grid).
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">StereoRoPE and wind vector rotation together should make learned operators transferable across grid topologies. To test this, we compare the native SCREAM cubed-sphere grid used during training with zero-shot rollouts on two unseen discretizations: a latitude–longitude grid and a rotated oblique stereographic grid. Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.4 Grid invariance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows 3-hour forecasts over Indonesia. The precipitation and humidity fields remain qualitatively consistent across these discretizations, showing that the model generalizes to unseen grid topologies without retraining. The agreement is not exact—interpolation, masking, and grid resolution differ across the three setups—but the spatial organization of precipitation and moisture is preserved across substantial changes in grid geometry.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">STRATA is the first AI model to simulate storm-scale atmospheric dynamics globally, expanding the prior state of the art of 900 km domain and 2-hour rollouts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> to the full planet and 24-hour rollouts, at 4.9 km and 10-minute resolution. Rollout evaluation confirms realistic simulation across the planet, spanning diverse convective regimes—from shallow marine stratocumulus and isolated continental storm lifecycles to organized deep convection, topographic precipitation, diurnal island convection, and midlatitude frontal bands.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At a <math id="S5.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="50\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\times</annotation></semantics></math> improvement in energy efficiency over SCREAM (the physics model it emulates) and a throughput of 741 simulated days per wall-clock day at 512 H100 GPUs, STRATA demonstrates that convection-resolving simulation can be generated affordably at planetary scale. Our analysis has revealed emulating convective dynamics requires <math id="S5.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\sim}10\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>10</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}10\times</annotation></semantics></math> more FLOPs per grid point than synoptic-scale forecasting, due to the higher information entropy of 3D convective dynamics. This provides a quantitative framework for future high-resolution atmosphere emulator design.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The current local-tile model learns convective-scale physics well but not large-scale circulation.
Coupling with a complementary low-resolution global emulator is a natural way to explore the next frontier, enabling century-scale simulations that quantify how the <em id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">frequency</em> of extreme weather events changes with environmental conditions.
Eventually, we hope the efficiencies of AI simulation might unlock the global <math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}</annotation></semantics></math>10-100-m scales needed to directly resolve low-cloud feedbacks—a major driver of climate sensitivity uncertainty <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> that remains computationally intractable
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Data and Code Availability</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The STRATA code, including the model architecture and training and inference pipelines, is available at <a href="https://github.com/NVlabs/STRATA" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/NVlabs/STRATA</a>. The raw SCREAM output used for training and evaluation is available at <a href="https://portal.nersc.gov/archive/home/n/ndk/www/STRATA2026" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://portal.nersc.gov/archive/home/n/ndk/www/STRATA2026</a>. As E3SM model output, it is distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license (see <a href="https://docs.e3sm.org/e3sm_data_docs/_build/html/index.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://docs.e3sm.org/e3sm_data_docs/_build/html/index.html</a>). A machine-learning training-ready version of the dataset in Zarr format will be released soon.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Background: Global Storm-Resolving Models</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Traditional climate models use approximate representations
of small-scale processes like thunderstorms and cloud physics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>,
which are a major source of uncertainty in climate projections.
Physics-based Global Storm-Resolving Models (GSRMs)
operate at kilometer-scale resolutions (<math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="&lt;5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">&lt;5</annotation></semantics></math> km)
to explicitly resolve deep convection and complex orography,
demonstrating superior fidelity in capturing
precipitation extremes, diurnal cycles,
and mesoscale organization compared to coarser models
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>.
However, their staggering computational and energy costs
fundamentally limit their utility
for large ensembles needed to optimally calibrate uncertain physics parameterizations and to sample internal variability alongside long-term ocean-coupled climate projections.
Recent supercomputing initiatives represent the state of the art:
the nextGEMS project demonstrated the feasibility
of 30-year coupled simulations
at 5–10 km resolutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>,
while SCREAMv1 achieved 419.5 simulated days per day
at 3.3 km resolution,
requiring 8,192 nodes of the Frontier supercomputer
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.
The EU Destination Earth initiative
has operationalized coupled multi-decadal digital twins
on EuroHPC systems,
achieving 120–230 simulated days per day
at 5–10 km resolutions
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>.
Despite these milestones,
the computational demands remain immense,
requiring dedicated access to the world’s largest supercomputers.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Architecture details</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A2.F1" title="Figure S1 ‣ B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a> summarizes the production architecture used for
the rollout results, and Table <a href="#A2.T1" title="Table S1 ‣ B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a> lists its main hyperparameters
and inference cost. The base DiT backbone produces patch-resolution semantic tokens,
while the de-aliasing decoder refines the output at full horizontal resolution.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.31248v1/dit-schematic.svg" id="A2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/198;" width="381" height="198"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S1: </span>Architecture of the STRATA with DiT backbone and PixelDiT-style pixel-space de-aliasing decoder.
<span id="A2.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(a)</span> The DiT backbone applies alternating 3D neighborhood attention
(NA3D) and column-wise (CW) attention for transformer blocks with StereoRoPE position
embeddings, followed by an unpatchify projection.
<span id="A2.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(b)</span> The pixel de-aliasing pathway re-embeds at full resolution and
applies NA3D blocks conditioned via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN)
on the backbone output, then projects to the output fields.
<span id="A2.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(c)</span> Each AdaLN block uses bilinear upsampling, depthwise (DW)
Conv2d with GeLU activation and RMSNorm, and a linear projection.
<math id="A2.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>base</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{base}}</annotation></semantics></math>: backbone embedding dimension; <math id="A2.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d_{\mathrm{pix}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>pix</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{\mathrm{pix}}</annotation></semantics></math>:
decoder embedding dimension.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table S1: </span>Architecture hyperparameters and inference cost of STRATA.
Inference measured on a single H100 80 GB GPU with <span id="A2.T1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torch.compile</span> and
BF16 mixed precision, batch size 1, tile size 64x64.</figcaption>

<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Patch-Size and Model-Size Sweep</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A2.T2" title="Table S2 ‣ B.2 Patch-Size and Model-Size Sweep ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a> defines the nine configurations used in the patch-size
and model-size scaling study in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Architecture ‣ 3 Proposed Method ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Model names
encode the FLOP tier (S/M/L) and horizontal patch size. Within each tier, depth
and width are adjusted so that models have approximately matched forward-pass
FLOPs while varying tokenization.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">PixelDiT-S (same FLOP tier as DiT-S, <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}1.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>1.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}1.2</annotation></semantics></math> TFLOP) and PixelDiT-M (
same FLOP tier as DiT-M, <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}5</annotation></semantics></math> TFLOP) add a standard PixelDiT decoder with
linear-projection upsampling to the corresponding DiT tier.
PixelDiT-M shares the same backbone hyperparameters as Table <a href="#A2.T1" title="Table S1 ‣ B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a>
but uses the original PixelDiT decoder with linear-projection upsampling
(i.e., Figure <a href="#A2.F1" title="Figure S1 ‣ B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a>c replaced by a single linear projection).
PixelDiT-S uses a smaller backbone: 768 embedding dimension, 14 transformer
layers, 12 attention heads, <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4\times 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4\times 1</annotation></semantics></math> patch size; pixel decoder:
64 embedding dimension, 2 transformer layers.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table S2: </span>Model configurations for the scaling sweep.
Model names encode FLOP tier (S/M/L) and horizontal patch embedding size
(e.g., DiT-S-ps4 is the smallest FLOP tier with <math id="A2.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> horizontal patch embedding).
Within each FLOP tier, the number of layers and hidden dimension are adjusted to match
the target FLOP budget; training hyperparameters are held fixed across all configurations.
All these nine models use an NA3D kernel size of 3; the PixelDiT and production models later adopted
kernel size 9 following further exploration (Table <a href="#A2.T1" title="Table S1 ‣ B.1 STRATA Architecture and Production Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a>).
</figcaption>
<table id="A2.T2.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="A2.T2.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="A2.T2.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A2.T2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Model</span></th>
<th id="A2.T2.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A2.T2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Layers</span></th>
<th id="A2.T2.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A2.T2.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Hidden dim <math id="A2.T2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math></span></th>
<th id="A2.T2.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="A2.T2.2.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">TFLOPs</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A2.T2.2.2" class="ltx_tr">

<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Patch De-aliasing</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Patch-size-4 tokenization makes transformer inference substantially cheaper by
operating on fewer horizontal tokens, but direct decoding can introduce a
periodic patch-scale mode during rollout. This artifact is easiest to see in
smooth near-surface fields such as <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{2\mathrm{m}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{2\mathrm{m}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Figure <a href="#A2.F2" title="Figure S2 ‣ B.3 Patch De-aliasing ‣ Appendix B Architecture details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a>
compares model variants at 12 h lead time: direct unpatchifying produces a
visible <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> checkerboard, while the PixelDiT-style two-stage decoder
reduces but does not fully remove patch-boundary structure. Our de-aliased
decoder replaces the original PixelDiT linear upsampling with bilinear
upsampling followed by a depthwise convolution, substantially reducing the
artifact while preserving the large-scale temperature structure.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/t2m_grid_4col_12row.png" id="A2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:238/597;" width="238" height="597" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S2: </span>Near-surface temperature (K) at 12 h lead time for 12 different locations
comparing four model variants.
<span id="A2.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DiT-M-ps4</span>: patch-size-4 DiT without de-aliasing,
showing visible checkerboard artifacts at the <math id="A2.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4\times 4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times 4</annotation></semantics></math> patch scale.
<span id="A2.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PixelDiT-M-ps4 (baseline)</span>: PixelDiT without the de-aliasing conditioning,
where patch-boundary artifacts persist.
<span id="A2.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PixelDiT-M-ps4 (dealiased)</span>: full STRATA de-aliasing decoder,
producing spatially smooth fields consistent with the reference, although on a small portion of locations, the patch-scale artifacts are not fully fixed.
<span id="A2.F2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SCREAM</span>: high-resolution reference simulation.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Patch Instability Analysis</h3>

<div id="A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For simplicity we can focus on the one dimensional case of a length <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> sequence. Let the flattened state vector be given by <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in\mathbb{R}^{nc_{in}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in\mathbb{R}^{nc_{in}}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{in}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{in}</annotation></semantics></math> is the channel index. For simplicity, we focus on a simple network consisting of <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Lx=DEx" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Lx=DEx</annotation></semantics></math> representing a linearized transformer model with a residual connection. Let <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> be the patch-size. The embed operator <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> represents patch embedding and can be expressed in matrix form as <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E=diag([W_{E},\ldots,W_{E}])" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E=diag([W_{E},\ldots,W_{E}])</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{c\ell\times c_{hid}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{c\ell\times c_{hid}}</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{hid}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{hid}</annotation></semantics></math> is the embedding dimension of the architecture. The decoding operation can also be expressed as a block-diagonal matrix <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=diag([W_{D},\ldots,W_{D}])" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=diag([W_{D},\ldots,W_{D}])</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{hid}\times c_{out}\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_{hid}\times c_{out}\ell}</annotation></semantics></math>. Putting this together we see that <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> also has a block diagonal form <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=diag([W_{L},...,W_{L}])" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=diag([W_{L},...,W_{L}])</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A2.SS4.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{L}=W_{D}W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{L}=W_{D}W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is a linear setting for ease of analysis. Moreover, it does represent an actual mode when there is a skip connection directly around the transformer blocks as in our architecture.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For any time marching procedure (e.g. weather rollout or diffusion sampling) the typical setup is to roll out the network recursively with dynamics given by</p>
<table id="A2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j+1}=Ax_{j}:=\alpha I+\beta Lx_{j}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j+1}=Ax_{j}:=\alpha I+\beta Lx_{j}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> are scalars or more generally diagonal matrices which repeat every <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{out}l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{out}l</annotation></semantics></math> elements. Setting <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0,1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0,1</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to state and tendency prediction, respectively. We note that <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is also block diagonal with all the blocks being <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{A}=\alpha I+\beta W_{D}W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{A}=\alpha I+\beta W_{D}W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math>.
It is an elementary fact that when initialized with non-degenerate initial data <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> such an iteration converges as <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{j}\rightarrow\lambda^{j}v_{1}\langle x_{0},v\rangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><msup><mi>λ</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{j}\rightarrow\lambda^{j}v_{1}\langle x_{0},v\rangle</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> is the eigenvector of <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> whose eigenvalue <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\lambda|=\rho(A)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\lambda|=\rho(A)</annotation></semantics></math> has the largest norm, also known as the spectral radius. This is known as the power-iteration algorithm. The <em id="A2.SS4.p2.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">stability region</em> of the iteration is defined as the subset of <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(W_{E},\alpha,\beta,W_{D})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(W_{E},\alpha,\beta,W_{D})</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A2.SS4.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For any block diagonal matrix like <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>, we can show that <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)=\rho(W_{A})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)=\rho(W_{A})</annotation></semantics></math> and that corresponding eigenvectors <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> have patch-scale structure. To see this, let <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> be an eigenvector of <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> with eigenvalue <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> be one of the patches, and <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x[i\ell:(i+1)\ell]=v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x[i\ell:(i+1)\ell]=v</annotation></semantics></math> (in Python notation) is the vector whose value is <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> in patch <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and zero elsewhere. Then, we see that <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is an eigenvector of <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>. i.e. <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Ax=[0,\ldots,0,W_{A}v,0\ldots,0]=[0,\ldots,0,\lambda v,0\ldots,0]=\lambda x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Ax=[0,\ldots,0,W_{A}v,0\ldots,0]=[0,\ldots,0,\lambda v,0\ldots,0]=\lambda x</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, the eigenvalues of <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> are also eigenvalues of <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, and in particular the largest one <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)=\rho(W_{A})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)=\rho(W_{A})</annotation></semantics></math>. Because the same block <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is repeated in every patch, the leading eigenspace of <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> consists of patch-local copies of the dominant eigenvector of <math id="A2.SS4.p3.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus power iteration amplifies the same within-patch pattern independently in each patch, producing a visible patch-scale artifact; the amplitude (and, for complex eigenvalues, phase) in each patch is determined by the projection of the initial state onto that patch’s eigenvector.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For typical neural network initializations, we see that <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math> which means that a periodic patch-scale artifact will dominate the rollout. By the considerations above the spectral radius of A is</p>
<table id="A2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)=\max_{m}\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta\Re\lambda_{m})^{2}+(\beta\Im\lambda_{m})^{2}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>m</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msqrt><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℜ</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℑ</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)=\max_{m}\sqrt{(\alpha+\beta\Re\lambda_{m})^{2}+(\beta\Im\lambda_{m})^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS4.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>λ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> are the eigenvalues of <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{D}W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{D}W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This explains why tendency prediction (<math id="A2.SS4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=1</annotation></semantics></math>) is observed to be less stable than state prediction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.
In this case, <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math> if <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{D}W_{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{D}W_{E}</annotation></semantics></math> has any eigenvectors with a positive real component, something that is almost sure to happen.
Even state prediction <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0</annotation></semantics></math> can be unstable for typical network initializations. With <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=1</annotation></semantics></math> the spectral radius <math id="A2.SS4.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)=\rho(W_{D}W_{E})\approx 2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>E</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)=\rho(W_{D}W_{E})\approx 2</annotation></semantics></math> when using Kaiming initialization of the weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Like any initial bias this can be trained away given enough data, but this is more efficient for high frequency fields that project strongly onto sub-patch scale variations. To see why, we note that the projection of the input data <math id="A2.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> onto <math id="A2.SS4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> can be bounded by <math id="A2.SS4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\langle x_{0},v\rangle|\leq||x-AvgPool_{\ell}x||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\langle x_{0},v\rangle|\leq||x-AvgPool_{\ell}x||</annotation></semantics></math>, assuming <math id="A2.SS4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is 0-centered. For smooth fields <math id="A2.SS4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="||x-AvgPool_{l}(x)||\ll||x||" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>≪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">||x-AvgPool_{l}(x)||\ll||x||</annotation></semantics></math> since the sub-patch variation only accounts for a small portion of the overall variance of the field. So, the component of single-step network prediction explained by patch artifact <math id="A2.SS4.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho(A)\langle x_{0},v\rangle v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ρ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho(A)\langle x_{0},v\rangle v</annotation></semantics></math> is small compared to the target magnitude <math id="A2.SS4.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Std[x]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Std[x]</annotation></semantics></math> and so is not suppressed quickly during training.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.5 </span>Additional Stabilization Details</h3>

<section id="A2.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">QK normalization and gated attention.</h4>

<div id="A2.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training in BF16 precision introduces attention instability: unconstrained query–key dot products can produce
pre-softmax logits on the order of <math id="A2.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 100</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="A2.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm 1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm 1000</annotation></semantics></math>, causing gradient overflow.
We address this with QK RMSNorm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>, which applies RMSNorm
(without learnable scale) to the query and key vectors before their dot product,
bounding the logit magnitude and enabling stable BF16 training. All attention blocks additionally use gated attention <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite>,
which applies a head-specific sigmoid gate to the attention output,
improving expressiveness and further stabilizing training.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Dataset details</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">STRATA is trained to emulate the Simple Cloud-Resolving E3SM Atmosphere
Model (SCREAM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. We use
native SCREAM physics-grid output without regridding. Prognostic 3D fields have
global shape <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(6,24,2048,2048)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>24</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2048</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2048</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(6,24,2048,2048)</annotation></semantics></math> on the cubed-sphere grid; prognostic and
diagnostic 2D fields have shape <math id="A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(6,2048,2048)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2048</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2048</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(6,2048,2048)</annotation></semantics></math>; boundary forcing 2D fields share the
same horizontal shape. Output is saved every 10 minutes.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>STRATA Vertical Grid</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SCREAM’s 128-level vertical grid is aggressively subsampled for the emulator.
We retain 24 levels spanning the troposphere and tropopausal layer
(approximately <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}100</annotation></semantics></math> hPa down to the surface in hybrid sigma-pressure coordinates),
discarding the stratosphere and above.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.31248v1/vertical_levels.svg" id="A3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:215/232;" width="215" height="232"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S3: </span>Pressure (hPa, in SCREAM’s hybrid sigma-pressure coordinates) of the 24 STRATA vertical levels,
indexed from the top of the atmosphere (level 1, <math id="A3.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}100</annotation></semantics></math> hPa) to the
surface (level 24, <math id="A3.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}1000</annotation></semantics></math> hPa). Dashed lines mark standard reference
pressure levels.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Training Data</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use three SCREAM simulations summarized in Table <a href="#A3.T3" title="Table S3 ‣ C.2 Training Data ‣ Appendix C Dataset details ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S3</span></a>.
The <em id="A3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sdecadal</em> simulation is initialized on 1994-10-01 and runs for
14 days.
The <em id="A3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">DYAMOND1</em> and <em id="A3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">DYAMOND2</em> simulations are initialized on
2016-08-01 and 2020-01-20, respectively, each running for 7 days.
For all three simulations, the first 24 h are excluded due to model spin-up.
The subsequent 9 days of sdecadal (1994-10-02 to 1994-10-10) and 4 days each
of DYAMOND1 (2016-08-02 to 2016-08-05) and DYAMOND2 (2020-01-21 to
2020-01-24) are used for training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The sdecadal simulation has an inconsistency: while the atmospheric initial
condition is from October 1994, the SSTs were erroneously prescribed from
October 2020 conditions.
We acknowledge this as a dataset error.
Nevertheless, we retain this simulation for training because SCREAM’s
underlying physics solver is unchanged and operates consistently regardless
of the IC–SST combination; each time step is physically self-consistent and
represents a valid atmospheric state evolution produced by the same numerical
model used for all other simulations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T3" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation initializations.</h4>

<div id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All rollout evaluations use 6 ensemble members initialized from the
held-out portion of the sdecadal simulation (after the training period
ends on 2020-10-10), at 12-hourly intervals:
2020-10-11 12:00, 2020-10-12 00:00, 2020-10-12 12:00,
2020-10-13 00:00, 2020-10-13 12:00, and 2020-10-14 00:00 UTC.
Note that dates are reported as 2020 to reflect the prescribed SST
conditions, though the atmospheric initial conditions are from October 1994.
Unless otherwise noted, single-run snapshot visualizations use the
2020-10-13 00:00 UTC initialization.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/covariance_comparison.png" id="A3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/243;" width="476" height="243" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S4: </span>Correlation coefficient matrices of <math id="A3.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x(t+\Delta t)-x(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x(t+\Delta t)-x(t)</annotation></semantics></math> for SCREAM (left) and ERA5 (right).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Input and Output Variables</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The model ingests six 3D prognostic fields (potential temperature, zonal and meridional wind, geopotential height, vertical pressure velocity, and specific humidity) on all 24 vertical levels, plus 2-m temperature and five forcing fields (solar zenith angle, latitude, surface geopotential, topography, and land fraction).
Most prognostic variables are predicted as tendencies <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta x=x_{t+\Delta t}-x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta x=x_{t+\Delta t}-x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>; vertical pressure velocity is predicted as absolute state due to lower variance. Diagnostic outputs include precipitation fields and surface pressure.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table S4: </span>STRATA input and output variables. “3D” variables have 24 vertical
levels; “2D” variables are single-level. Prediction mode applies only to
prognostic variables: <em id="A4.T4.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">tendency</em> means the model predicts
<math id="A4.T4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta x=x_{t+\Delta t}-x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta x=x_{t+\Delta t}-x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>; <em id="A4.T4.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">state</em> means the model predicts
<math id="A4.T4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t+\Delta t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t+\Delta t}</annotation></semantics></math> directly.</figcaption>
<table id="A4.T4.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A4.T4.6.1" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="A4.T4.6.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="A4.T4.6.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Dims</span></td>
<td id="A4.T4.6.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt"><span id="A4.T4.6.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Role</span></td>
