<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table S6: </span>Differential entropy (bits/dim) of spatial patches assuming a Gaussian distribution. The entropy of white noise <math id="A10.T6.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma=I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma=I</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="A10.T6.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}(2e)\approx 2." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}(2e)\approx 2.</annotation></semantics></math> For ERA5 this analysis uses the same 72 output channels as FCN3<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A11" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix K </span>Additional sensitivity test</h2>

<section id="A11.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">K.1 </span>Width versus Depth Scaling</h3>

<div id="A11.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a fixed compute budget (FLOPs), should one prefer a wider model (larger embedding dimension) or a deeper one (more layers)?
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. [18]</a></cite> find that global weather forecasting models consistently favor increased width over depth,
a trend that differs from behavior observed in language models.
We examine whether this holds across the full range of model sizes relevant to STRATA.</p>
</div>
<div id="A11.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A11.F14" title="Figure S14 ‣ K.1 Width versus Depth Scaling ‣ Appendix K Additional sensitivity test ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S14</span></a> shows test loss as a function of model scale under iso-FLOP width and depth sweeps.
At smaller model sizes, scaling width outperforms scaling depth at matched FLOPs, consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. [18]</a></cite>.
We interpret this as the embedding dimension being a bottleneck at small scale:
a narrow model lacks sufficient channel capacity to represent the diverse atmospheric variables and their interactions,
so increasing width provides a larger per-token information budget that depth alone cannot compensate.
At larger model sizes, however, this advantage reverses: deeper models show a slight edge over wider ones at matched FLOPs.
This large-FLOP regime is not covered by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. [18]</a></cite>, and our results suggest that once the embedding
dimension is wide enough to carry the necessary information, additional depth provides more expressive power per FLOP.
These findings informed our choice of the STRATA architecture, which uses a relatively wide semantic encoder paired with a moderate number of layers.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A11.F14" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/figures/sweep_width_ablation.jpg" id="A11.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/260;" width="476" height="260" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S14: </span><span id="A11.F14.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Width vs. depth scaling at fixed FLOPs.</span>
Test loss as a function of model size for iso-FLOP sweeps that increase width (embedding dimension)
or depth (number of layers).
At small model sizes, wider models outperform deeper ones, consistent with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. [18]</a></cite>.
At larger model sizes, deeper models show a marginal advantage, a regime not explored in prior work.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A11.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">K.2 </span>Inference Tile Size</h3>

<div id="A11.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using a large tile size at inference is advantageous because it means there is less computation wasted on the halo regions.
However, since the model was fine-tuned with a differing tile size of 128, there is some risk of exposure bias when running it with larger tile sizes only for inference. Figure <a href="#A11.F15" title="Figure S15 ‣ K.2 Inference Tile Size ‣ Appendix K Additional sensitivity test ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S15</span></a> shows that using a larger padded size “tile size + 2 halo” during inference results in a marginally worse dry bias especially in the tropics. However, the difference is small compared to the overall bias versus the ground truth.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A11.F15" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.31248v1/tile_size_sweep.svg" id="A11.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/197;" width="357" height="197"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S15: </span>Precipitation bias at 12 hour lead time for various tile and halo sizes during inference.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A11.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">K.3 </span>Effective Batch Size and Training Tile Size</h3>

<div id="A11.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Larger training tiles increase the effective batch size, since each tile covers more samples of independent storms.
However, large-batch training is known to exhibit diminishing returns: beyond a critical batch size,
increasing the batch further yields no improvement in convergence per unit of data processed,
and may even degrade final loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>.
This raises the question of whether km-scale atmospheric emulation benefits from the very large batch sizes
that large tiles would provide.</p>
</div>
<div id="A11.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To answer this, we perform a batch size sweep on the SCREAM dataset, scaling the learning rate linearly
with batch size following the linear scaling rule <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>. All samples are <math id="A11.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 64</annotation></semantics></math> tiles.
As shown in Figure <a href="#A11.F16" title="Figure S16 ‣ K.3 Effective Batch Size and Training Tile Size ‣ Appendix K Additional sensitivity test ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S16</span></a>, training with batch sizes up to 32 is stable, and smaller batch sizes achieve marginally lower test loss when evaluated
at equal total number of training samples—consistent with the large-batch generalization gap reported
in prior work.
Increasing the batch size beyond this regime leads to training instability: the linear learning rate
scaling rule breaks down, and loss diverges or fails to converge, indicating that the gradient noise
at smaller batch sizes plays a beneficial regularization role that cannot simply be compensated by a
proportionally larger learning rate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A11.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Together, these results suggest that training on moderate tile sizes (<math id="A11.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 64</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A11.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="128\times 128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>128</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">128\times 128</annotation></semantics></math>)
is not only computationally efficient but also well-matched to the effective batch size regime where
optimization is most stable.
As mentioned in the main text, this is further supported by the physics of the problem: at a 10-minute timestep, the maximum range
of information propagation is bounded by the acoustic wave speed (<math id="A11.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}340" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>340</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}340</annotation></semantics></math> m/s), limiting the
physical context required within a single tile.
Large tiles therefore do not provide proportionally more useful physical context per training step,
reinforcing the case for compact, compute-efficient tiles.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A11.F16" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/figures/testloss-batchsize.png" id="A11.F16.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/160;" width="238" height="160" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S16: </span><span id="A11.F16.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Batch size ablation.</span>
Test loss as a function of batch size under linear learning rate scaling. Each
sample is a <math id="A11.F16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 64</annotation></semantics></math> tile.
Training is stable and achieves the lowest loss at batch sizes up to 32.
Smaller batch sizes show a marginal benefit in per-sample efficiency.
Beyond batch size 32, training becomes unstable as the linear scaling rule breaks down,
indicating a critical batch size beyond which further increases are counterproductive.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A11.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">K.4 </span>Model capacity and rollout stability</h3>

<div id="A11.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A11.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A11.F17" title="Figure S17 ‣ K.4 Model capacity and rollout stability ‣ Appendix K Additional sensitivity test ‣ Scaling Storm-Resolving Atmospheric AI Simulation to the Entire Planet" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S17</span></a> illustrates a characteristic failure mode
of the smaller FLOP-size model (<math id="A11.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}1.2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>1.2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}1.2</annotation></semantics></math> TFLOP) at 24-hour lead time.
Behind the dominant speckle of km-scale dynamics, the vertical velocity <math id="A11.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math> field shows large, coherent planetary-scale
anomalies—broad regions of anomalous ascent and
subsidence absent in both the SCREAM reference and the larger model rollouts.
These patterns are inconsistent with mass continuity, which requires
<math id="A11.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math> averaged over thousand-kilometer scales to remain near zero,
suggesting the smaller model lacks sufficient capacity to maintain
physically balanced large-scale circulation.
The specific humidity field shows a corresponding degradation: the
unrealistic large-scale descent drives spurious drying that further
degrades forecast quality.
Empirically, larger FLOP-size models are less prone to such artifacts at
24-hour lead times; however, a more principled constraint on large-scale
<math id="A11.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\omega" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ω</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\omega</annotation></semantics></math> is likely needed to ensure stability at longer horizons.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A11.F17" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.31248v1/size_compare_face1_frame143_omega25-qv25_rmse.png" id="A11.F17.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/200;" width="333" height="200" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure S17: </span><span id="A11.F17.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rollout skill on smaller vs larger models.</span>
Snapshots of several fields (vertical velocity, specific humidity) for small (1.2 TFLOP, left) and middle (4.9 TFLOP, middle) FLOP-size models and reference SCREAM ground truth (right) at 24-hour rollout lead time. The smaller model shows more pronounced artifacts with larger humidity RMSE. RMSE values of vertical velocity and specific humidity are reported on the forecast panels are evaluated on 4<math id="A11.F17.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> coarsened fields for the shown cube face to focus more on large-scale error instead of pixel-wise agreement.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</article>
